newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally, with Dow setting record.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally, with Dow setting record.

text.p: Stocks rallied for the second straight session Monday, pushing the Dow Jones industrial average to its 14th record of the year.
The dollar ended lower, oil prices fell, gold rose and bonds were little changed.
The 30-share Dow jumped 78.50 points to 7,079.39 after adding 56 points on Friday on a government report of solid job growth in February with little sign of wage-driven inflation.
Companies with strong brand names and oil producers led the way, and the market got a boost from news of the latest surge of cash into mutual funds, investors and analysts said.
"It looks like the big boys are back buying the big stocks," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
The Dow close eclipsed the previous record of 7,067.46 set on Feb. 18 though most other major market gauges remained well off record levels. The Dow set 44 records for all of 1996.
In the broader market, winners beat losers, 1,639 to 856, on moderate New York Stock Exchange volume of 458.7 million shares.
Bargain-hunting helped high-technology stocks shake off their recent woes, though most of Monday's gains were confined to bigger blue-chip issues.

News of a fresh surge of cash into mutual funds also helped stocks, analysts said. Americans ploughed $1.49 billion into funds for the three days ended on Thursday, up from $7 million for the two days ended on March 3, said Mutual Fund Trim Tab, which tracks the data. Figures often vary widely.
As in the past, fund managers seemed to be pouring the new cash directly into big stocks, analysts said.
But in a departure from recent sessions, investors seemed to be sifting through the technology sector, looking for bargains created by the group's recent sell-off.

The Nasdaq composite index, heavily weighted with technology stocks, rose 10.92 points to 1,322.72, a smaller percentage gain than that posted by the Dow and one that kept it well below its record of 1,388.06 set on Jan. 22.
In currency trading, the dollar fell against the German mark as remarks by German and Italian officials fuelled growing doubts that a single European currency will be launched as planned in 1999.
In late New York trading, the dollar stood at 1.7015 marks, down from 1.7140 marks late on Friday. The dollar fell to 121.63 Japanese yen from 121.90 yen.
Crude oil prices fell, with the April contract falling 79 cents to $20.49 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
April gold added $3.20 to $352.70 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
The 30-year Treasury bond was little changed, leaving its yield at 6.82 percent.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose 17.1 points to a record 4,437.4. Tokyo's Nikkei average of 225 stocks lost 84.85 points to 18,113.89.
